title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: From the moment he received this news until the end of the campaign, all of Kutuzov's activity was directed toward restraining his troops—by authority, by cunning, and by pleading—from useless attacks, maneuvers, or encounters with the dying enemy. Dokhturov went to Malo-Yaroslavets, but Kutuzov lingered with the main army and gave orders for the evacuation of Kaluga—a retreat beyond that town seemed entirely possible to him.
Everywhere Kutuzov retreated, but the enemy, without waiting for his retreat, fled in the opposite direction.

Napoleon's historians describe to us his skillful maneuvers at Tarutino and Malo-Yaroslavets and speculate about what would have happened if Napoleon had managed to penetrate into the rich southern provinces in time.

But setting aside the fact that nothing prevented him from advancing into those southern provinces (the Russian army wasn't blocking his way), the historians forget that nothing could have saved his army, because it already carried within itself the seeds of inevitable destruction. How could that army—which had found abundant supplies in Moscow and had trampled them underfoot instead of preserving them, and on reaching Smolensk had looted provisions instead of storing them—how could that army recover in Kaluga province, inhabited by the same kind of Russians who had lived in Moscow, where fire had the same property of consuming whatever was set ablaze?
That army could not recover anywhere. Since the Battle of Borodino and the pillaging of Moscow, it had carried within itself, as it were, the chemical elements of dissolution.

The members of what had once been an army—Napoleon himself and all his soldiers—fled without knowing where, each concerned only with escaping as quickly as possible from this position, of the hopelessness of which they were all more or less vaguely conscious.

So at the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, when the generals pretended to deliberate and offered various opinions, all mouths were shut by the opinion of the simple-minded soldier Mouton, who spoke last and said what they all felt: the one thing needful was to get away as fast as possible. And no one—not even Napoleon—could argue against that truth they all recognized.

But though everyone realized they had to retreat, there remained a feeling of shame at admitting they had to flee. An outside jolt was needed to overcome that shame, and it came in due time. It was what the French called 'the Emperor's hurrah'—le hourra de l'Empereur.

The day after the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, Napoleon rode out early among the lines of his army with his suite of marshals and an escort, ostensibly to inspect the troops and the scene of the recent and upcoming battle. Some Cossacks out looking for plunder ran into the Emperor and very nearly captured him. If the Cossacks did not capture Napoleon then, what saved him was the very thing that was destroying the French army—the booty on which the Cossacks fell. The Cossacks went after the plunder, just as they had at Tarutino, leaving the men behind. Ignoring Napoleon, they chased the booty, and Napoleon managed to escape.

When les enfants du Don—the children of the Don, the Cossacks—could so easily have captured the Emperor himself in the midst of his army, it was clear there was nothing to do but flee as fast as possible along the nearest, familiar road. Napoleon, with his forty-year-old stomach, understood the hint. No longer feeling his former agility and boldness, and shaken by the fright the Cossacks had given him, he immediately agreed with Mouton and issued orders—as the historians tell us—to retreat along the Smolensk road.

That Napoleon agreed with Mouton, and that the army retreated, doesn't prove that Napoleon caused it to retreat, but that the forces influencing the entire army and directing it along the Mozhaysk (that is, the Smolensk) road were simultaneously acting on him as well.
